meta.title: Who really said "When you stop talking, you've lost your customer. When you turn your back, you've lost her"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Widely credited to Estée Lauder and true to how she sold, but no primary source has been located for this exact wording. We say so rather than invent one.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When you stop talking, you've lost your customer. When you turn your back, you've lost her'?
meta.ogDescription: A sales maxim credited to Estée Lauder. Consistent with her counter selling — but unsourced, and we could not pin it to any book or interview.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1908–2004 · American cosmetics entrepreneur · co-founder of Estée Lauder
answer.sourceLine: This is credited to Estée Lauder almost everywhere it appears, and it fits what she is actually documented as having done — selling face to face from the very beginning. What we could not do is pin the wording to a source. There is no Wikiquote page for her, Quote Investigator ↗ has not investigated the line, and the quotation sites that carry it give no citation we were able to check. Her 1985 autobiography Estée: A Success Story is the obvious place for it, but the only copy we could reach ↗ is lending-restricted, so we could not search it. We are recording this as attributed, not verified, and asserting no source.

source.excerpt: When you stop talking, you’ve lost your customer. When you turn your back, you’ve lost her.
trail: Wikipedia’s article on Estée Lauder ↗ establishes the person and the plausibility: an American businesswoman (1908–2004) who co-founded the company with her husband, and the only woman on Time’s 1998 list of the twenty most influential business geniuses of the twentieth century. It does not carry this quotation.

The Internet Archive’s catalogue record for Estée: A Success Story ↗ confirms the 1985 Random House edition of her autobiography. The scan is lending-restricted and returned no searchable text, so we could not confirm or rule out the line in it.

We searched for a primary citation and found none: no Wikiquote page exists for her, and the quotation aggregators that carry the line supply no verifiable source. On a site whose whole claim is provenance, that absence is the finding — so this page says “attributed” and stops there rather than borrowing a citation it has not read.
source.cutTag: The line as it circulates — no earlier form is documented
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller context to show, because no source text has been located. The two sentences travel together in this form wherever they appear, and we have not found a version that differs — which is weak evidence either way: a line that only ever appears in quotation collections has no provenance, just repetition.
source.rightsNote: We could not identify the work this wording first appeared in, so we assert no rights status. Estée Lauder died in 2004 and anything she published is in copyright; nothing on this page is offered as public domain.

author.bio: Estée Lauder was an American businesswoman who co-founded her eponymous cosmetics company with her husband, Joseph Lauter. She built it by selling in person — opening counters herself, giving away samples, and treating the face-to-face encounter as the whole of the business — and by 1998 she was the only woman on Time’s list of the twenty most influential business geniuses of the twentieth century. The company she started now owns brands from Clinique to La Mer.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The maxim is really a description of a technique. Wikipedia’s account of her career ↗ has her selling face to face from the very beginning: she “began selling the preparation to her friends”, then sold creams “to beauty shops, beach clubs and resorts”, and “returned to the beauty parlor… to demonstrate their use”. Her own summary of herself was blunter: “I have never worked a day in my life without selling.” Read against that, the line is less advice than a rule she enforced on herself — keep talking, never turn away.

It is also a good illustration of why this site exists. A sentence can be perfectly in character, repeated for decades, and still have no traceable origin. Being plausible is not the same as being sourced, and the honest page says which of the two it has.

sourcesVerified.claim: Estée Lauder (1908–2004) was an American businesswoman who co-founded the cosmetics company with her husband and was the only woman on Time’s 1998 list of the 20 most influential business geniuses of the 20th century.
Estée: A Success Story was published by Random House in 1985 (catalogue record confirms the edition; the scan is lending-restricted and does not confirm the quotation).

Wikipedia documents Lauder selling face to face: she began selling to her friends, sold creams to beauty shops, beach clubs and resorts, returned to the beauty parlor to demonstrate their use, and said "I have never worked a day in my life without selling." It does NOT describe counter selling, free samples or a "tell a woman" method.
